Every key factual claim traces to a licensed source via inline link: Spain's 2-0 win over France from THE STORY; the Porro 58th-minute goal linked to AP News as cited in THE STORY; the Mbappé "lack of communication" quote attributed and linked to the Reuters source named in THE STORY; the Nature player-tracking research and the PLOS ONE passing-network research both linked exactly as they appear in the source text. The PLOS ONE DOI suffix `10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0171156` is reproduced faithfully in the URL (the faithfulness-gate number). No invented events, quotes, numbers, people, or causal mechanisms appear. The triangles-in-basketball analogy (Phil Jackson, 1987–1998, Tex Winter's triangle offence, Chicago Bulls) is drawn directly from THE STORY without embellishment. The lede names the event concretely in its first sentence and the demand lens (geometry, space, football, final) is expressed naturally throughout the body rather than forced. The "will" prohibition is respected: the body uses "may" and "could" rather than "will" for forward-looking statements. No rhetorical questions appear. The ending opens outward without predicting. The "As [X] notes/reports" template is used twice, within the permitted limit, with varied constructions elsewhere. **Headline — PASS** The headline carries the source article's own organizing terms and is produced by the `source-title-fallback` mechanism, which is appropriate and faithful. **Lede — PASS** The lede (one paragraph, approximately 90 words) names the event, venue, and stakes in the first sentence, then establishes the analytical question the article develops. Acceptable. **Section structure — PASS WITH NOTE** Four sections build a single analysis: the geometry of the semi-final triangles, the probabilistic space model, the cross-sport triangle principle, and what the analysis implies for Argentina. Each section continues the prior argument without restating the event. The demand-lens warning (`demand-lens-missing-h2`) from the deterministic standards is acknowledged; "The shape that conquered basketball" signals the geometry frame through "shape" and "A pitch made of probabilities" signals the spatial/quantitative frame. The warning does not rise to a required repair on its own. **Material failures requiring revision** *Description field.* The current value is: "Spain face Argentina in the FIFA World Cup final this Sunday at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey." This is approximately 80 characters and carries no analytical hook. The form exemplar targets approximately 113 characters and requires the description to convey the article's distinctive angle — here, Spain's geometric space-control system and what it means for the final. A reader seeing this description in a feed or search result learns nothing that distinguishes this article from any match preview. This is a material metadata defect. *Summary field.* The current summary runs approximately 84 words across three sentences. The form requirement specifies approximately 53 words. The third sentence (recording both sides' rankings and titles) is factually accurate but padds the count, and the second sentence can be tightened. Trimming to target does not require removing the article's key analytical points. *Final section context usage.* "What Argentina must answer" opens with two distinct attributed facts drawn from CONTEXT 1 — Argentina's tactical identity (compact defense, rapid counter-attack through Messi) and their semi-final win over England — before pivoting to THE STORY's concluding observation. The pipeline instruction limits a context item to "one explicitly attributed fact or comparison." Two attributed facts from one context item in a single section gives that item more structural weight than the rule permits. This is repairable by compressing the Argentina tactical description into a single attributed sentence and moving immediately to THE STORY's geometry conclusion. **Fairness, harm, sensationalism — PASS** The article does not criticize a person or institution, allege wrongdoing, or report a dispute requiring a response opportunity. No needless harm, stereotyping, or commercial influence is detected. Reported analysis is distinct from advocacy throughout. **Failure layer diagnosis** The assignment, sources, and instructions were sufficient to produce a publishable manuscript. The body prose demonstrates this. The description and summary failures are execution errors against explicit form requirements stated in the prompt; the context-usage issue in the final section is an execution error against an explicit sourcing rule. Both are writer-model failures, not upstream defects in assignment or sources. A targeted replay of the three identified repairs produces a publishable manuscript without any structural changes to the body. Spain face Argentina in the FIFA World Cup final this Sunday at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, per [Geometry, football and the World Cup final](https://theconversation.com/geometry-football-and-the-world-cup-final-287792). [Both sides arrive unbeaten after seven matches](https://theconversation.com/tactically-complete-spain-vs-an-inspired-messi-led-argentina-who-will-win-the-world-cup-final-287372): Argentina as the defending champions and Copa América holders ranked first in the world, Spain as the reigning European champions ranked second. Attacking flair and physicality no doubt play a role, according to The Conversation's analysis of the final. But a tactical question the match raises is the one Spain's 2-0 semi-final victory over France made visible — how to solve a team that controls not just space, but the conditions under which space would next appear.

## Forcing choices

In the semi-final, Spain built passing triangles around French players with a precision that sometimes created the impression of numerical superiority on the pitch. Wherever a Spanish player received the ball, two teammates appeared at different angles, with French defenders consistently arriving a fraction too late to close down the options. The triangles mattered not because of their shape but because of the decision costs they imposed: each pass forced a French defender to commit to one possible future — press the ball, block the inside route, or protect the space behind. By the time that choice was made, the ball had often moved and the geometry had changed again. As [The Conversation's analysis of the match](https://theconversation.com/geometry-football-and-the-world-cup-final-287792) describes it, Spain was not simply finding space; the team was controlling when and where the next space would appear.

A useful football triangle does not require equal sides or 60-degree angles. Its best shape changes with ball speed, defender orientation, and the available pitch area. A narrow triangle is easy to squeeze because one defender can block both lanes; a wider triangle extends the pass, giving opponents more time to intercept. Against France, Spain found the middle ground repeatedly — close enough for quick combinations, but spread enough to stretch the French press across the full width it needed to cover.

## A pitch made of probabilities

Football geometry is a problem of time as well as space. A passing lane is not open simply because no defender is standing in it; the key question is whether the ball reaches a receiver before an opponent reaches the interception point. [Research using player-tracking data published in Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-021-97537-4) estimates control of the pitch from each player's position, direction, speed, and acceleration, producing a constantly changing map of who is most likely to reach each area first. The pitch, in this framing, is a probability surface rather than a static diagram.

Pedro Porro's [58th-minute goal against France](https://apnews.com/article/france-spain-world-cup-score-87fb7740fa552edf4bfd28d0e8727c23) demonstrated that principle in compact form. After exchanging passes with Dani Olmo, Porro continued his run to score Spain's second. The first pass shifted the defenders' attentional focus; Porro's movement created a new angle for the return before France could reset its defensive shape.

Three-player combinations extend this problem further. Spain's strength was not one triangle but the speed at which several overlapped — a midfielder functioning as a corner of multiple shapes simultaneously, linked to a defender, full-back, winger, and another midfielder at once. [Passing-network research published in PLOS ONE](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0171156) describes players as points and passes as links, but a final network diagram misses what mattered most against France: Spain rebuilt those links with every movement and first touch. The value of each pass lay not only in where the ball went but in how it changed what could happen next. That is why ten sideways passes are not automatically better than one pass that pulls two defenders out of position.

## The shape that conquered basketball

Triangles are not unique to football. Under head coach Phil Jackson between 1987 and 1998, the Chicago Bulls made frequent use of what became known as [Tex Winter's triangle offence](https://www.hoophall.com/hall-of-famers/tex-winter), placing three players on one side of the court to create passing, cutting, and scoring options simultaneously. The sport differed but the structural principle was the same: triangles preserve alternatives. Close one route and another remains; follow the ball and space opens elsewhere.

France's problem against Spain was not a lack of effort. Pressing works only when several defenders move together and close connected passing options at the same time. After the semi-final, Kylian Mbappé [attributed France's defensive breakdown to "a lack of communication" in the pressing](https://www.reuters.com/sports/soccer/spain-choke-life-out-france-reach-world-cup-final-2026-07-14/). Spain kept moving before France could reorganise — changing the shape of the problem faster than the opposition could solve it. The triangles were visible on the pitch; their real advantage was control over what could happen next.

## What Argentina must answer

The Conversation's [pre-final analysis](https://theconversation.com/tactically-complete-spain-vs-an-inspired-messi-led-argentina-who-will-win-the-world-cup-final-287372) describes Argentina as a side built on compact defending and rapid counter-attacks routed through Messi. To press Spain's triangles, Argentina must sustain the co-ordinated defensive communication France could not maintain. To defend deeper is to accept the kind of geometric control Spain demonstrated against France — the ability to determine when and where the next space would appear.

The analysis that mapped Spain's semi-final geometry concludes that Argentina are expected to study their opponents' tactics closely before the final, and that geometry may play a prominent role in the championship match — and may prove a deciding factor. The specific open question as Sunday approaches is whether Argentina's preparation has produced a workable answer to a passing system that, against France, appeared to have none.
